  • Higher borrowing costs weigh hardest on heavily indebted France, whose debt-to-GDP ratio was 119% in the second quarter, according to the national statistics institute
  • The bank sees three possible brakes on spread widening: a sharp fall in oil prices, a dovish ECB shift such as slower quantitative tightening, or a credible fiscal plan after the May 2027 presidential election
  • Goldman cautions that oil depends on Middle East developments, that ECB action would likely need much more market disorder, and that the fiscal fix is still some way off
  • It is neutral on French rates, saying the widening offers some value but the outlook is uncertain, and constructive on European rates overall given its benign inflation view

France’s sharp bond market repricing reflects a rate shock that began with energy prices and has since become more entrenched, according to Goldman Sachs, which sees only a handful of ways to bring the French-German spread back under control.

In a note setting out three questions on the widening, the bank said the initial rise in rates driven by elevated energy prices has turned more structural as strong economic data push up estimates of the neutral interest rate, the level at which policy neither stimulates nor restrains the economy. Goldman said higher borrowing costs can be particularly punishing for heavily indebted countries such as France, whose debt-to-GDP ratio reached 119% in the second quarter of 2026, according to the national statistics institute.

The bank said rising French yields point to growing market concern about the country’s fiscal path, particularly in a higher-for-longer rate environment and with political uncertainty building ahead of next year’s presidential election. The French premium over German debt reached its widest level since the 2011 eurozone debt crisis earlier this month, at close to 160 basis points, before easing back toward the 130s, according to market reports.

Goldman identified three developments that could rein in the widening. The first is a sharp fall in oil prices, which would naturally pull bond yields lower, though the bank cautioned this cannot be relied on given its dependence on events in the Middle East. The second is a dovish shift from the European Central Bank to ease financial conditions, which Goldman said could come without rate cuts, for example by slowing quantitative tightening. It added, however, that markets would likely need to become much more disorderly before such tools are used. ECB officials have so far signalled that intervention is not yet warranted. The third is an improving fiscal outlook, with a credible consolidation plan after the May 2027 presidential election and the parliamentary elections likely to follow. Goldman noted this remains relatively distant.

On positioning, Goldman said it is neutral on French rates. The spread widening has created some value, it said, but the situation remains uncertain. Across Europe more broadly, the bank holds a constructive view on rates, arguing that the degree of monetary tightening priced in is unwarranted given its benign inflation outlook.

With oil exposed to Middle East risk, the ECB reluctant to step in and the fiscal reset tied to an election more than six months away, the bank’s analysis suggests French spreads may stay sensitive to headlines well into next year.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: More on Standard Chartered adding RLUSD custody in Dubai, eyes LMAX collateral link for clients
item.description:
The announcement is more a signal about market structure than a price catalyst. Bank custody does not create direct demand for RLUSD or for XRP, and traders should not read it that way. The bigger question is competition. If regulated banks start offering off-exchange margin, smaller stablecoins with bank backing could win institutional business that has so far gone to the largest tokens. Venues may also come under pressure to offer similar setups once a mirrored model proves itself, which could change how collateral moves across crypto trading.

---

Earlier:

  • Standard Chartered custody for Ripple’s RLUSD: what custody and collateral mirroring mean for traders

---

Standard Chartered is offering to hold Ripple’s stablecoin and let clients trade against it without the tokens ever reaching an exchange, but the trading half of that promise still needs regulators to sign off.

Summary:

  • Standard Chartered now offers institutional custody of RLUSD on the XRP Ledger through its DIFC branch, regulated by the DFSA.
  • A planned integration with LMAX Group would make RLUSD eligible collateral on agreed LMAX products through “collateral mirroring.”
  • Under mirroring, the tokens stay at the bank while LMAX credits their value toward client positions.
  • The LMAX leg is not live and still needs final documentation, testing and regulatory approval, with no launch date given.
  • RLUSD has a market value of about $2.45 billion, under 1% of a roughly $306 billion stablecoin market.
  • The bank has offered crypto custody in Dubai since 2024 and in July began letting institutions mint and redeem USDC directly.

Standard Chartered has begun offering institutional custody for Ripple’s dollar-backed stablecoin RLUSD through its branch in the Dubai International Financial Centre, and is preparing a link with LMAX Group that would let clients use the tokens as trading collateral without moving them off the bank’s books. The British lender said on Monday that eligible clients can now hold the XRP Ledger version of RLUSD on its digital asset custody infrastructure, with the service run from its DIFC branch under the supervision of the Dubai Financial Services Authority.

The second part of the announcement is the more consequential, though it is not yet operational. Standard Chartered has joined a planned integration with LMAX, the London-based currency and crypto marketplace, that would make RLUSD eligible margin on agreed LMAX products. Under a structure the bank calls collateral mirroring, the stablecoin would remain in custody at Standard Chartered while LMAX receives a mirrored record of its value that counts toward a client’s positions. The bank said the arrangement still depends on final documentation, testing and regulatory sign-off, and it gave no date for when clients will be able to post RLUSD as margin.

The design is aimed at the counterparty risk that comes with leaving collateral on a trading venue. If an exchange were to fail under the mirrored model, the client’s tokens would still be held at Standard Chartered, one of 29 banks the Financial Stability Board treats as globally systemically important and subjects to tougher capital requirements. Waqar Chaudry, who leads digital assets within the bank’s securities services business, said institutions want exposure to digital asset markets without weakening the protection around their holdings.

RLUSD, which Ripple launched in December 2024 on Ethereum and the XRP Ledger, is backed by US dollars, US government bonds and cash equivalents. It received approval from the Dubai regulator in June 2025 and has grown to a market value of roughly $2.45 billion, still under 1% of a stablecoin market worth about $306 billion.

The move extends a broader push by the bank into digital assets. Standard Chartered has provided crypto custody in Dubai since 2024, and in July said it had become the first global systemically important bank to let institutions mint and redeem Circle’s USDC directly. The timing and terms of LMAX approval will now determine whether the mirroring model moves from concept to a working margin product.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Saudi Arabia eyes 1.2 million bpd pipeline boost within weeks by converting gas line
item.description:
A quick 1.2 million bpd addition to bypass capacity would ease some of the supply-risk premium built into crude, since it widens the route Saudi barrels can take around a disrupted Strait of Hormuz. The bearish oil price read is tempered by execution risk: the same corridor was knocked offline by a drone strike only last month, and Houthi attacks keep the Red Sea leg exposed. Port capacity at Yanbu is the bigger constraint for traders to watch, because extra pipeline volume only reaches the market if loadings can keep pace. Taken together, the plan signals that Riyadh expects disruption at Hormuz to persist, and that is supportive of prices over the longer run even if the near-term supply outlook improves at the margin.

----

Earlier:

  • Big Monday recap ... Oil gains on two fronts as Russia hits Ukraine and Saudi vows Houthi response

---

Riyadh is reaching for the fastest lever it has to get more crude around Hormuz, though the real bottleneck may sit at the Red Sea port rather than in the pipe.

Summary:

  • Saudi Arabia is examining plans to raise pipeline crude export capacity to 10 million bpd, according to comments attributed to Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman
  • He said converting a gas pipeline to carry crude could add 1.2 million bpd within seven to eight weeks
  • The Energy Ministry has said reaching the full 10 million bpd target would take two to three years
  • The 7 million bpd East-West pipeline was shut in September after a drone strike launched from Iraq, and was carrying close to 6 million bpd by 6 October
  • Riyadh has been rerouting around 4 million bpd, roughly 4% of global supply, to Yanbu since the US-Iran war disrupted Hormuz shipments
  • Ship-tracking data suggest Yanbu can load only around 4.5 million bpd, a potential constraint on extra exports

Saudi Arabia is examining plans to raise its pipeline crude export capacity to 10 million barrels per day, with Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman saying the conversion of a gas pipeline to carry crude could add 1.2 million bpd within seven to eight weeks.

The comments point to a fast-track first step toward a longer-term goal. The Saudi Energy Ministry has said it expects lifting oil pipeline capacity to 10 million bpd to take two to three years, so the gas line conversion would deliver a meaningful increase well ahead of any full expansion.

The push reflects how central the East-West pipeline has become to Saudi exports. The line runs from fields and processing facilities near the Gulf to the Red Sea port of Yanbu and has a capacity of around 7 million bpd. Since the US-Iran war disrupted shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, Riyadh has been using it to reroute around 4 million bpd to Yanbu, according to Reuters, equivalent to about 4% of global supply.

That route has itself come under attack. The pipeline was shut in September after a drone strike launched from Iraq, which Saudi Arabia blamed on Iraqi militias. Argus reported, citing sources, that three of the line’s 11 pumping stations were damaged, one of them significantly, although the pipeline itself was not. On 6 October, Prince Abdulaziz said flows had recovered to close to 6 million bpd, with operations restarting within about a week of the attack. Separately, Aramco shut its 400,000 bpd Jizan refinery on the Red Sea coast after a Houthi attack in early September.

Expansion talk is not new. Reuters reported earlier, citing sources, that the kingdom was considering adding 1 million to 2 million bpd of East-West capacity, potentially including the ability to carry refined products.

Port capacity may prove the binding constraint. Ship-tracking data indicate Yanbu can load only around 4.5 million bpd, well below the pipeline’s nameplate capacity. Any additional pipeline volumes will therefore depend on matching gains at the terminal end.

The plan also suggests Riyadh is preparing for prolonged disruption at Hormuz, with markets now watching for details on which line would be converted, the timeline for terminal upgrades, and the security of a corridor that has already been struck once.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Standard Chartered custody for Ripple’s RLUSD: what custody and collateral mirroring mean for traders
item.description:
Standard Chartered will now hold Ripple’s dollar-pegged stablecoin, RLUSD, for institutional clients through its branch in the Dubai International Financial Centre. The bank also plans to let those clients use RLUSD as trading collateral at LMAX Group without the tokens ever leaving the bank. That second part is not live yet. Together, though, the two pieces show how traditional finance is trying to fix one of crypto’s oldest problems: what happens to your money when the venue holding it fails.

To see why this matters, it helps to unpack three ideas: stablecoins, custody and collateral.

What happened

The bank announced on Monday that it now supports institutional custody of RLUSD issued on the XRP Ledger. The service runs through its DIFC branch, which is regulated by the Dubai Financial Services Authority. Separately, Standard Chartered has joined a planned integration with LMAX Group, a London-based marketplace for currencies and crypto, that would make RLUSD eligible collateral on agreed LMAX products.

What is RLUSD?

A stablecoin is a crypto token designed to hold a steady value, in this case $1. RLUSD is backed by US dollars, US government bonds and cash equivalents. Ripple launched it in December 2024 on both Ethereum and the XRP Ledger, a public blockchain closely associated with Ripple. The bank’s new service covers only the XRP Ledger version.

RLUSD has grown to a market value of roughly $2.45 billion. That sounds large, but it is still less than 1% of a stablecoin market worth about $306 billion. It is a small player in a field dominated by much bigger tokens.

What custody actually means

Custody is the unglamorous plumbing of finance. A custodian is a regulated institution that keeps your assets safe and is legally responsible for them. In crypto, that usually means the custodian controls the private keys needed to move the tokens.

There is a trade-off. Handing assets to a custodian adds protection, but it also means the custodian sits between you and your funds. Because it operates under regulation, it can be required to monitor, freeze or restrict assets in its care. For institutions, that oversight is usually a feature rather than a drawback, because their own rules often require assets to be held by a regulated party.

Collateral and the exchange problem

When traders use leverage, they must post collateral, also called margin. This is a safety deposit the trading venue holds against possible losses.

Traditionally in crypto, that collateral sits with the exchange itself. If the exchange collapses, traders can become unsecured creditors waiting to recover their money. The 2022 collapse of FTX made that risk painfully clear to the market.

How collateral mirroring works

Standard Chartered’s answer is what it calls collateral mirroring. Under the planned set-up, the RLUSD stays at the bank. LMAX receives a mirrored record of its value, and that value counts toward the client’s trading positions. The tokens themselves never move to the exchange.

The practical effect is a separation between where you trade and where your assets live. If the exchange ran into trouble, the trader’s collateral would still be sitting at Standard Chartered, one of 29 banks the Financial Stability Board classes as globally systemically important and subjects to stricter capital rules.

The bank’s head of digital assets in securities services, Waqar Chaudry, said institutions want access to digital asset markets without weakening how their assets are protected. That is the core pitch: trade on the venue, keep the money at the bank.

What this does and does not mean

It is worth being precise about what has changed. Custody of RLUSD is live for eligible clients. The LMAX collateral arrangement is only planned. The bank said it still depends on final documentation, testing and regulatory approvals, and it gave no date for when clients could post RLUSD as margin.

This is also not Standard Chartered buying RLUSD or XRP. Offering custody is a service, not an investment. Readers should be careful not to treat it as a direct source of demand for XRP, the separate token linked to the XRP Ledger.

The move does fit a pattern. Standard Chartered has offered crypto custody in Dubai since 2024, and in July it said it became the first global systemically important bank to let institutions mint and redeem Circle’s USDC directly. RLUSD received approval from the Dubai regulator in June 2025.

What to watch next

The key milestone is the LMAX integration going live. Watch for confirmation that testing and regulatory approvals are complete, and which LMAX products will accept RLUSD as collateral.

Also watch whether RLUSD’s market value keeps growing relative to the wider stablecoin market. Bank-grade custody could make it more attractive to institutions, but a move from under 1% to a meaningful share would be the real evidence of demand.

What could change the picture: delays or conditions attached to the LMAX approval, or other large banks offering similar mirroring arrangements for bigger stablecoins, which could leave RLUSD’s advantage short-lived.

The lesson for traders is straightforward. Where your collateral sits matters as much as where you trade. Collateral mirroring is one attempt to separate the two, and it is worth understanding before it becomes standard practice.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: JPMorgan says Q3 earnings will support stocks as growth spreads beyond AI
item.description:
The call argues for broadening rather than narrowing equity exposure, with near-record numbers of stocks seeing accelerating earnings suggesting leadership need not rest on a handful of AI names. For Europe, recent derating in banks and French equities sets a lower bar into results, leaving room for relief rallies if earnings simply hold up. The bond market is the swing factor: a peak in yields as reporting gets under way would remove the main headwind to valuations, while a further leg higher would test the thesis. Companies flagging rising energy costs also tie the earnings outlook back to crude, so any renewed oil spike is a direct risk to European margins.

---

Earlier:

  • US stocks close mixed

--- JPMorgan reckons the headline earnings bar looks scarier than it is, and that once results start rolling in, September’s jitters should give way to fundamentals that still hold up.

Summary:

  • JPMorgan strategists led by Mislav Matejka expect third-quarter earnings to support markets, with strength broadening beyond AI despite investor concern after weeks of volatility
  • S&P 500 consensus sees Q3 EPS growth of 24% on IBES data (30% on FactSet and LSEG after a Meta tax adjustment), falling to 15% excluding Nvidia and Micron and 8% for the median stock
  • European consensus is 19%, dropping to 11% excluding energy, with a median of 9%; median revenue growth is 7% on both sides of the Atlantic
  • Global PMIs hit multi-year highs in the quarter, and JPMorgan’s lead indicator points to at least two more positive reporting seasons
  • European margins are seen around 14% of sales this year, 250 basis points above 2019, with energy likely to beat while miners, China and consumer exposure lag
  • JPMorgan stays positive on European semiconductors, banks, chemicals and industrials, and sees a peak in bond yields opening the way for equity gains into year-end

Third-quarter earnings should reassure investors and act as a support for equities, according to JPMorgan strategists, who say profit strength is broadening beyond artificial intelligence even as many investors fear results will disappoint after weeks of market volatility.

The team, led by Mislav Matejka, said investors already hold a constructive view on earnings, but argued that results will still underpin the market. Expectations look elevated at face value, the strategists said, yet appear more reasonable on closer inspection. Consensus for S&P 500 earnings per share growth in the quarter stands at 24% on IBES data. FactSet and LSEG put the figure at 30% because of an adjustment for a one-off tax charge at Meta. Excluding Nvidia and Micron, the growth hurdle falls to 15%, and for the median stock it drops to 8%.

In Europe, consensus is for 19% growth, easing to 11% once energy is stripped out, with a median of 9%. Median revenue growth is running at 7% for both the S&P 500 and the Stoxx 600.

JPMorgan pointed to global purchasing managers’ indexes, which accelerated during the quarter to multi-year highs and are consistent with strong earnings. The bank’s own lead indicator for earnings is still rising and typically runs about two quarters ahead, which the strategists said suggests at least the next two reporting seasons should be positive. AI continues to carry much of the load in the US, they said, but the share of global stocks with accelerating earnings is close to a record, which should improve the odds of a durable upcycle.

In Europe, margin expansion is doing most of the work, with operating margins projected at around 14% of sales this year, some 250 basis points above 2019 levels. Every sector is improving except staples, autos and software. A weaker euro should help exporters, and energy is likely to surprise to the upside. Miners are a risk, China and consumer exposure may remain soft, and companies are likely to flag rising energy costs.

The strategists also expect strong results from semiconductors and industrials. Banks have derated, meaning their valuation multiples have fallen, by more than 10% in recent weeks but should still report reassuring earnings. French equities have derated by more than 15% even as profits hold up, though the CAC 40 earns three quarters of its revenue outside France.

Looking ahead, JPMorgan said the recent spike in bond yields is nearing oversold territory. If yields peak as the reporting season begins, equities could climb into year-end with risk-on internals, the strategists said. The bank remains positive on European semiconductors, banks, chemicals and industrials, and expects market focus to shift from September’s volatility toward fundamentals that remain supportive. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed’s Hammack says more tightening needed to cool demand, keeps open mind on pace
item.description:
Hammack’s remarks reinforce the hawkish tilt within the Fed and keep the possibility of a back-to-back hike alive, even though markets currently expect a hold in October. Her explicit focus on AI-driven capex and wealth effects puts high-flying tech equities in the crosshairs, since tighter policy aimed at curbing investment and asset-fuelled spending works partly through valuations. The comments should lend support to the dollar and front-end Treasury yields, while also weighing on gold, which has tended to fall as rate hike expectations build. Traders will watch whether other voters echo her view that the inflation fight now targets demand directly rather than the labour market.

---

Hammack wants to take some heat out of a booming economy without burning the labour market, and she is open about which part of demand she would prefer to cool first.

Summary:

  • Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack said she believes interest rates need to move higher to restrain demand and bring down inflation, which she sees stuck in a 2.5% to 3.0% range
  • She said she will approach the October 27-28 meeting with an open mind on whether to hike again after September’s increase; markets currently expect a hold
  • Hammack hopes tighter policy can cool corporate investment or wealth-driven consumption without pushing unemployment above the current 4.2%
  • She warned an inflationary psychology may be taking root, with AI-related investment pressures spreading beyond data centres to other firms
  • Business contacts are describing a booming economy rather than preparing to pull back, according to Hammack, who is a voter this year and dissented in July in favour of a hike

Cleveland Federal Reserve President Beth Hammack said on Monday she believes US interest rates need to rise further to restrain demand. She also said she hopes the Fed can bring inflation down without damaging a labour market that remains close to full employment.

In an interview with Reuters, Hammack said demand is being driven both by a rapid pace of corporate investment and by market-driven wealth gains that are supporting consumer spending, factors she sees as keeping inflation lodged in a range of 2.5% to 3.0%. In her view, restrictive monetary policy could cool those forces enough for inflation to fall without unemployment rising beyond the current 4.2%. She said she is not trying to stop growth, only to slow it to a pace that eases pricing pressure. A pullback in either business investment or consumption would help, she added, and restraint on the capital spending side might mean less of the burden falls on consumers.

Hammack said she would go into the Fed’s October 27-28 meeting with an open mind on whether another hike is warranted after September’s increase. She feels more restriction is needed, she said, but considers the timing an open question. Hammack is a voter on rate policy this year and dissented in July in favour of a hike, while investors currently expect the Fed to hold in October. Her remarks are among the most explicit from a Fed official about using restrictive policy to cool demand directly.

With inflation high and the labour market stable, Hammack said the Fed is being challenged on only one side of its mandate. She wants to address inflation deliberately so that employment is not weakened unnecessarily. In her assessment, consumer spending is being held up largely by higher-income households and the wealth effect.

Hammack said business contacts sound more like they are describing a booming economy than preparing to retrench. She is concerned that an inflationary psychology may already be taking root among firms competing for resources, as relentless investment by AI hyperscalers leaves cost a secondary concern. Executives, she said, are planning for inflation to stay high and expect to raise prices faster than their input costs. In her view, the pressure that began with data centres is now spreading more broadly.

Hammack described monetary policy as a single blunt instrument that she intends to use judiciously, in the right amount and at the right speed, while maintaining that more restraint is needed. Her comments leave the October decision finely balanced between market expectations of a pause and a hawkish core of policymakers who see a case for tightening further.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman Sachs flags power and compute as two chokepoints in the AI boom
item.description:
The note points investors toward the physical layer of the AI trade, with access to high-voltage power now a tighter constraint than the capital to buy chips. That favours operators that have already secured grid capacity, and it suggests power availability, more than chip supply, could set the pace of new data centre builds through 2027. In software, budgets moving toward data and cybersecurity point to a widening gap between foundational platforms and application vendors, whose pricing models could come under pressure as agents replace human users. The emphasis on core platform returns also implies investors may reward proven monetisation of compute over speculative new revenue lines.

---

In Goldman’s reading of the AI boom, money can buy the GPUs, but power decides who gets to switch them on.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs says demand for AI infrastructure keeps outpacing capacity, and the compute supply-demand gap is widening, based on its discussions with tech company management teams
  • A likely slowdown in model training is being offset by rising investment in AI safety and pacing monitoring, which keeps compute demand elevated
  • Leading hyperscalers are securing power contracts for 2028 and beyond because grid capacity for 2026 and 2027 is essentially fully booked
  • Capex is rising on component inflation and the need for more chips, while revenue generated per unit of power has risen by around two-thirds over the past year
  • Goldman sees data and security platforms among the clearest beneficiaries of AI spending, and says application software is increasingly being built for AI agents rather than people
  • Meta is generating two to three times return on investment per megawatt in its core business, and Google is using a full-stack approach spanning custom silicon, cloud, security and distribution

Demand for AI infrastructure continues to run ahead of available capacity, and the bottleneck is moving from chips toward power, according to Goldman Sachs, which drew on recent discussions with the management teams of technology companies.

The bank said the gap between compute supply and demand is widening, driven by new infrastructure requirements and resilient enterprise spending. Goldman expects model training to slow, but it said companies are stepping up investment in AI safety and pacing monitoring, work that needs more computing power and so keeps overall compute demand high.

In Goldman’s view, power has become the defining constraint. Grid capacity for 2026 and 2027 is essentially booked out, the bank said, and leading hyperscalers are therefore moving aggressively to secure power contracts for 2028 and beyond. Goldman argued that having the capital to buy GPUs is no longer enough on its own, and that access to high-voltage energy infrastructure now decides who can expand. Capital expenditure is climbing on component inflation and demand for more chips. Over the same period, revenue generated from each unit of power has risen by around two-thirds compared with earlier price points over the past year.

The bank also described a structural shift in enterprise software. It believes data and security platforms are among the clearest beneficiaries of AI spending, because AI depends on clean, organised and secure data. Chief information officers are increasingly steering budgets toward foundational data layers and cybersecurity tools, aiming to protect data integrity and contain the risks of unsanctioned “shadow AI” use inside organisations.

Application software is going “headless”, meaning it is increasingly being designed for AI agents rather than human users. Goldman said this lets vendors build more powerful AI features into existing platforms and supports industry growth for now. It cautioned, however, that the change could eventually alter how software companies price and monetise their products.

Among the companies it highlighted, Goldman said Meta continues to generate two to three times return on investment per megawatt of power in its core business while exploring new sources of incremental revenue. Google, the bank said, is relying on a full-stack advantage that combines custom silicon, cloud, security and a vast distribution base to drive core monetisation. In that picture, sales of its TPU chips are one part of a broader portfolio strategy.

Goldman concluded that AI monetisation offers substantial optionality. Even so, in its view core platform monetisation remains among the higher-confidence and higher-return uses of compute, which suggests the established platforms that already earn strong returns on their power may stay the more dependable beneficiaries as capacity remains scarce. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: investingLive Americas FX news wrap 12 Oct: USD climbs, EURUSD hits a 2026 low as oil rises and stocks finish mixed
item.description:
• US stocks close mixed
  • Earnings calendar October 12–16: Big banks, ASML and TSMC take center stage
  • Hammack de la Fed: Las tasas del Tesoro son “modestas” según los estándares históricos
  • European stocks close higher. Spain leads while the dollar strengthens
  • Gold falls toward hourly moving averages. Can sellers keep control?
  • Bitcoin buyers had their shot above the 200-hour MA. They missed.
  • investingLive European session wrap: Oil rebounds, dollar firms as US bond market holiday keeps traders cautious
  • Morning Kickstart: Dollar higher, oil rebounds as holiday trading begins

The dollar had the stronger hand to start the trading week. EURUSD traded to a new low for the year, while USDJPY moved above its 200-day moving average and stayed above. Oil advanced, precious metals retreated, and U.S. stocks finished mixed.

It was a holiday session with an important piece missing: the U.S. cash Treasury market was closed. There was no fresh bond-market reaction to the higher oil price or hawkish comments from Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack. That reaction will have to wait until Tuesday.

Dollar higher across the board

In the supplied late-session snapshot, the dollar was higher against all seven major currencies. Its largest gain was against the Swiss franc, while its smallest gain was against the Canadian dollar.

  • EURUSD: 1.1155, −0.41%.

  • USDJPY: 158.64, +0.21%.

  • GBPUSD: 1.3203, −0.21%.

  • USDCHF: 0.8345, +0.53%.

  • USDCAD: 1.4280, +0.18%.

  • AUDUSD: 0.6955, −0.39%.

  • NZDUSD: 0.5584, −0.34%.

EURUSD broke below last week’s low at 1.11603. The buyers had their shot earlier when the rally reached 1.1217 near the falling 100-hour moving average. They could not get above that ceiling, and sellers pushed to fresh lows.

The next downside target is 1.11296, the 50% midpoint of the rally from January 2025 to January 2026. Holding below the 100-hour moving average near 1.12056 keeps sellers in control.

For USDJPY, the 200-day moving average at 158.54 is the nearby barometer. Stay above, and the bias remains more bullish. Move back below, and today’s break loses some of its strength. Can the buyers keep the momentum going in the new trading day?

Treasury market closed

The following are Friday’s closing yields, carried into Monday’s holiday session:

  • 2-year: 4.7911%.

  • 5-year: 5.0211%.

  • 10-year: 5.2421%.

  • 30-year: 5.6001%.

There is no Monday cash-market basis-point change to report. Elevated borrowing costs remain part of the backdrop, but Tuesday will provide the first fresh Treasury response to Monday’s developments.

U.S. stocks close mixed

The Dow advanced, while the broader indices finished lower. The Nasdaq 100 led the declines.

  • Dow industrial average: 51,856.18, +196.00 points, +0.38%.

  • S&P 500: 7,807.24, −4.30 points, −0.06%.

  • Nasdaq Composite: 27,245.90, −120.27 points, −0.44%.

  • Russell 2000: 2,794.48, −12.50 points, −0.45%.

  • Nasdaq 100: 30,664.70, −218.45 points, −0.71%.

The divergence shows an uneven market heading into earnings season. Large Nasdaq-listed shares lagged, but the index snapshot alone does not establish which sectors or individual companies drove the move.

European stocks finish higher

European equities enjoyed a firmer start to the week, led by Spain:

  • Germany’s DAX: 25,277.69, +0.76%.

  • France’s CAC 40: 7,832.89, +0.38%.

  • UK’s FTSE 100: 10,656.28, +0.99%.

  • Spain’s Ibex 35: 19,285.79, +1.33%.

  • Italy’s FTSE MIB: 50,034.99, +0.58%.

Hammack keeps the inflation debate alive

With no major U.S. economic releases, Beth, Cleveland Fed president, supplied the main policy headline.

Her message leaned hawkish. She sees a need for additional restraint and is concerned about early signs that inflation expectations could become less anchored. A higher neutral rate would also imply that current interest rates may restrain activity less than their level alone suggests.

However, she acknowledged the pressure on lower-income households and the risks to employment. The debate she outlined is about the pace of further tightening, with the jobs side of the mandate still part of the balancing act.

Oil rises; metals and Bitcoin retreat

The supplied late-session snapshot showed:

  • WTI crude futures, CL1!: $93.21, +$1.36, +1.48%.

  • Gold, XAUUSD: $4,169.99, −$24.655, −0.59%.

  • Silver: $60.2222, −$0.5568, −0.92%.

  • Bitcoin: $82,969, −$710, −0.85%.

Oil remained sensitive to Middle East tensions. InvestingLive’s afternoon coverage reported renewed tension accompanying the push to fresh highs. Higher energy prices keep inflation risk in focus, although the closed Treasury market prevents assessing a same-day cash-yield response.

Gold’s decline was consistent with the stronger dollar. Silver also fell, while Bitcoin’s retreat lined up with the weaker Nasdaq and small-cap indices. That is a similar direction for the session, without establishing a lasting relationship.

A busier week starts Tuesday

Major bank earnings begin Tuesday, followed by U.S. CPI Wednesday and PPI and retail sales Thursday. The reports will test inflation pressures, consumer spending and corporate performance.

For the next session, watch whether EURUSD sellers can extend toward 1.11296, whether USDJPY buyers can hold above 158.54, and how Treasury yields respond when trading resumes. The dollar has momentum. Now comes the test of whether it can keep it.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.
